source.title: Measurement of Energy Spectrum and Elemental Composition of PeV Cosmic Rays: Open Problems and Prospects

accepted.question_text: What physical sources, acceleration mechanisms, and propagation processes produce the observed population of cosmic rays, especially Galactic cosmic rays in and above the PeV range, given that the all-particle energy spectrum contains features such as the knee, second knee, ankle, and high-energy cutoff, but ground-based measurements still disagree in ways that may reflect unknown systematic uncertainties?

evidence.quote: More than one century after their discovery, we have no definitive models yet about the origin, acceleration and propagation processes of the radiation. The main reason is that there are still significant discrepancies among the results obtained by different experiments located at ground level, probably due to unknown systematic uncertainties affecting the measurements.

All the observed features are believed to carry fundamental information that sheds light on the key questions of the origin, acceleration and propagation of CRs. However, from the all-particle results alone, it is not possible to understand the origin of different features.

accepted.question_text: Which nuclear mass component is responsible for the all-particle cosmic-ray knee observed at about 4 × 10^15 eV: a cutoff of the light proton-plus-helium component at a few PeV, or an all-particle knee dominated by heavier nuclei after the light component has already cut off below about 1 PeV?

evidence.quote: All experiments observed the knee at about 4 × 1015 eV but a general consensus about the chemical component responsible for such a feature does not exist yet because experimental results are still conflicting, as will be discussed in Section 5.

Several experimental results associate the knee with the bending of the light component (p and He), and are compatible with a rigidity-dependent cut-off [22–24,53–55]. However, the flux of the different components vary significantly depending on the interaction model used to interpret the data [22–24]. On the contrary, other results (in particular those obtained by arrays located at high altitudes) seem to indicate that the knee of the all-particle energy spectrum is due to heavier nuclei and that the light component cuts off well below 1 PeV [21,26,31,52,53,56].

The elemental composition is conflicting. Experiments located at high and extreme altitude (BASJE-MAS, Tibet ASγ, ARGO-YBJ, EAS-TOP and CASA-MIA) reported evidence that the knee of the (p+He) component is below 1 PeV and that the composition at the all-particle knee energy is dominated by heavier nuclei. Experiments located deeper in atmosphere (KASCADE, KASCADE-Grande, IceTop/IceCube, Tunka-133) reported evidence that the proton knee is at the same energy of the all-particle knee.

accepted.question_text: Where does the Galactic cosmic-ray spectrum end, and at what energy does the transition from Galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays occur, once the energy-dependent elemental composition through the knee and toward 10^17–10^19 eV is measured accurately?

evidence.quote: Determining elemental composition in the knee energy region is crucial to understand where Galactic CR spectrum ends and to give a solid basis to CR models up to the highest observed energies.

Indeed, it is widely believed that the bulk of CRs up to about 1017 eV are galactic, produced and accelerated by the shock waves of SuperNova Remnants (SNR) expanding shells [9], and that the transition to extra-galactic CRs occurs somewhere between 1017 and 1019 eV.

accepted.question_text: Are supernova remnants capable of supplying the power and magnetic-field amplification needed to accelerate Galactic cosmic-ray protons to PeV energies and beyond, or must the main PeV cosmic-ray sources be a different class of Galactic accelerators?

evidence.quote: The experimental results, however, do not demonstrate the capability of SNRs to produce the power needed to sustain the population of galactic CRs and to accelerate particles up to the knee, and beyond. Indeed, to accelerate protons up to the PeV energy domain, a significant amplification of the magnetic field at the shock is required, but this process is problematic [10].

However, the first results reported by the LHAASO experiment [11,12], that is, the observation of a number of gamma sources emitting photons beyond 500 TeV, show that SNRs are likely not the main sources of PeV CRs in our galaxy.
The first PeVatrons observed in the northern hemisphere by the LHAASO experiment show that SNRs are probably not the main sources of PeV CRs in our galaxy.

accepted.question_text: For very-high-energy γ-ray sources, how can observations determine whether the γ-rays are produced by π^0 decay in hadronic cosmic-ray interactions or instead by relativistic electrons through inverse Compton scattering or bremsstrahlung, so that PeV cosmic-ray source candidates can be identified conclusively?

evidence.quote: Unlike neutrinos that are produced only in hadronic interactions of CRs, the question whether the observed γ-rays are produced by the decay of π0 from CR interactions (‘hadronic’ mechanism), or by a population of relativistic electrons via Inverse Compton scattering or bremsstrahlung (‘leptonic’ mechanism), still needs a conclusive answer.
Therefore, the quest for CR sources to be able to accelerate particles up to the PeV range in a multi-messenger approach requires the observation of the γ-ray sky above 100 TeV.

accepted.question_text: What unknown systematic uncertainties make direct, indirect, and ground-array measurements of the 100 TeV–100 PeV cosmic-ray spectrum and composition conflict, and how can experiment designs disentangle the effects of altitude, detector coverage, muon measurements, shower-core observables, reconstruction procedures, and hadronic-interaction models?

evidence.quote: In fact, important results obtained by ‘direct’ methods are conflicting due to some still unknown systematic uncertainties probably related to the interaction model used to assign the energy.

These results cannot be reconciled and show the existence of a still unknown systematic uncertainty that, as discussed in previous sections, could be due to the different array characteristics (altitude, coverage), the observables used (muons or shower core characteristics), and the dependence on hadronic interaction models.

The experimental situation in the 100 TeV–100 PeV energy region must be clarified to solve the longstanding problem of the origin of the knee and to give solid foundations to CR models up to the highest observed energies. A new experiment, able to measure, at the right altitude and with high statistics, the elemental composition exploiting the techniques used so far in different apparatus, is mandatory to investigate the unknown uncertainties affecting the results so far obtained by shower arrays.

accepted.question_text: How can air-shower-array analyses reconstruct primary cosmic-ray energy and mass composition in a way that is not merely a model-dependent consistency check, given the intrinsic degeneracy among primary energy, primary mass, and hadronic-interaction modeling, the lack of direct mass observables for most arrays, and shower-to-shower fluctuations?

evidence.quote: In fact, analysis of shower data consists in the disentanglement of a threefold problem involving primary energy, primary mass and modelling of hadronic interactions (for a discussion about hadronic interactions in CR physics see, as an example, refs. [47,48] and references therein).
Strictly speaking, when operating with shower arrays there are no observables directly related to the mass of the primary particle, and its measurement is very indirect.

Therefore, a typical data analysis consists in finding a combination of primary energy spectrum, elemental composition and hadronic interaction characteristics to obtain a consistent description of the experimental results. Clearly, this is not a measurement, but only a consistency check of some trial models. In case of discrepancy, it is difficult to identify the origin; in case of agreement, is the parameter combination unique?

accepted.question_text: If the knee and related spectral features follow a rigidity-dependent pattern, are they caused primarily by maximum acceleration energy at cosmic-ray sources or by inefficient Galactic confinement and escape, and what measurements of proton and other mass-group spectra up to about 10^17 eV can decide between these rigidity-acceleration and rigidity-confinement interpretations?

evidence.quote: The observed features in the all-particle energy spectrum seem to be consistent with the bending of different components in a rigidity-based scenario. However, rigidity models can be • rigidity-acceleration models, that is, the knee can be an acceleration feature, a source property, related to the maximum energy of particle acceleration inside the CR sources; • rigidity-confinement models, that is, the knee is related to inefficient confinement of particles in the galaxy. In this case, the galaxy could contain ’super-PeVatrons’, astrophysical objects able to accelerate particles well beyond the PeV.

In the coming years, the LHAASO experiment is expected to be able to measure the energy spectra of different mass groups up to 1017 eV and to determine the energy of the proton knee, thus clarifying the origin of the knee in the all-particle spectrum.

accepted.question_text: Can atmospheric-neutrino measurements above about 100 TeV distinguish between competing parent cosmic-ray proton spectra inferred by experiments such as ARGO-YBJ and KASCADE, despite the onset of an astrophysical neutrino component whose origin and experimental uncertainties are not yet understood well enough to draw clear conclusions?
accepted.context_brief: Atmospheric neutrinos as a proton-spectrum test

evidence.quote: Important information could be deduced, in principle, by the measurement of the flux of atmospheric neutrinos, sensitive to the spectrum of parent CRs. In particular, the tail of the spectrum of atmospheric neutrinos is mainly shaped by the parent protons rather than by heavier element.

As a consequence, we expect different predictions for the flux of atmospheric neutrinos according to ARGO-YBJ and KASCADE proton energy spectra, predictions that, in principle, can be checked at energies Eν ≥ 100 TeV if the atmospheric neutrinos could be properly identified.

Unfortunately, in this energy region the total neutrino flux detected by IceCube departs from the existing predictions for atmospheric neutrinos suggesting the onset of an astrophysical component. The origin of such neutrinos is still unknown and current experimental uncertainties do not allow to draw clear conclusions [71].

accepted.question_text: Which super-PeVatrons, if any, exist in the Inner Galaxy and Galactic Center regions, and what wide-field Southern Hemisphere observations are needed to monitor those regions and test whether they contain sources accelerating particles well beyond PeV energies?

evidence.quote: The observation of sources emitting photons above the PeV in the North suggests the need of a wide field of view instrument in the Southern Hemisphere to monitor the Inner Galaxy and the Galactic Center looking for super-PeVatrons (SWGO [77], STACEX [78]) to operate with CTA-South [79].

trace.notes: Normalized arXiv abs URL to https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.11618.pdf and downloaded the exact PDF artifact for extraction.

Mapped PDF sections: Abstract; Introduction; Detection Techniques; Extensive Air Showers; Reconstruction of Energy and Mass; Elemental Composition in the 10^14 to 10^18 eV Region; What's Next; Conclusions. Candidate open-problem regions were concentrated on pages 1-4, 17-19, and 23-25.
Extracted broad unsolved problems on cosmic-ray origin, the knee composition, Galactic-to-extragalactic transition, SNR PeV acceleration, and hadronic versus leptonic γ-ray emission.
Extracted unresolved systematic and reconstruction problems from direct/indirect measurement boundaries, model dependence, and the threefold energy-mass-hadronic-model degeneracy.
Extracted experimental conflicts over the light-component cutoff, p+He versus heavy dominance at the all-particle knee, and use of atmospheric neutrinos as an external test.

Extracted prospective unresolved questions about clarifying the 100 TeV-100 PeV region, distinguishing rigidity-acceleration from rigidity-confinement models, determining the proton knee, and surveying the Southern sky for super-PeVatrons.
Expanded the abstract and introduction statements into a self-contained question about CR source, acceleration, and propagation models.
Merged the repeated knee-composition conflict into one self-contained mass-component question covering p+He and heavier-nuclei alternatives.
Restated the Galactic endpoint and extragalactic transition issue using the paper's composition-dependence and 10^17-10^19 eV transition evidence.
Separated the SNR acceleration-capability problem from the γ-ray emission-mechanism problem because the paper gives distinct evidence for each.
Kept the hadronic-versus-leptonic γ-ray mechanism as a standalone multi-messenger source-identification question.
Expanded unknown systematic uncertainties into the specific experimental factors explicitly listed in the source: altitude, coverage, observables, and interaction models.
Converted the source's model-dependence discussion into an open methodological question about unique energy and mass reconstruction.
Restated the conclusion's two rigidity-model alternatives as a decisive-question formulation tied to mass-group and proton-knee measurements.
Included the atmospheric-neutrino test because the paper explicitly says the astrophysical neutrino component origin is unknown and current uncertainties prevent conclusions.
Included the Southern Hemisphere super-PeVatron search as an implicit open observational problem directly stated in the conclusions.

Merged near-duplicate statements about the knee origin, light-component cutoff, and composition conflict into q_002; kept q_003 and q_008 separate because they concern the Galactic endpoint and mechanism of rigidity scaling, respectively.

Accepted candidates have page-numbered verbatim evidence, no source-pointing phrasing in question_text, explicit solved-status metadata, and no unsupported definitions beyond the cited source statements. Didactic source questions in Section 4 about how arrays obtain spectra and composition were not accepted as open research questions because the source immediately answers them.
